items.headline: Lewica odmawia, KO czeka, PSL i Polska 2050 idą na rozmowy o TK
items.summary: po zaproszeniu Nawrockiego na poniedziałek Anna Maria Żukowska powiedziała, że "nic się nie zmieniło", a Mirosław Suchoń przypomniał, że poprzednie zaproszenie z 31 października nigdy nie dotarło.
items.matters: konsultacje startują z dziurą po dwóch największych klubach opozycji.
items.body: Szef Kancelarii Premiera Jan Grabiec pytany przez PAP, czy przedstawiciele Koalicji Obywatelskiej wezmą udział w spotkaniu, przekazał: "Odpowiemy, jak dotrze do nas zaproszenie". Z kolei w TVP Info Grabiec zwrócił uwagę, że politycy KO nigdy nie odmawiają, jeśli są zapraszani przez prezydenta. Zaznaczył jednak, że poniedziałkowe spotkanie ma prowadzić szef Kancelarii Prezydenta. Grabiec został też zapytany o nieobecność przedstawicieli KO podczas podobnego spotkania 31 października. Powiedział, że "zaproszenie nie dotarło, niestety pan prezydent nie zdecydował się wtedy spotkać z przedstawicielami Koalicji Obywatelskiej". - Dostaliśmy pytanie, czy ktoś z nas jest gotowy rozmawiać z panem prezydentem, podaliśmy nazwiska i Kancelaria Prezydenta zamilkła na długie godziny, więc chyba nie spodziewali się tego, że będziemy gotowi rozmawiać - stwierdził. W poniedziałkowym spotkaniu w KPRP udziału nie weźmie Lewica. - Nie, po tej informacji medialnej skonsultowałam się na szybko z członkami prezydium mojego klubu, jednomyślnie uważamy, że nic się nie zmieniło - powiedziała na antenie Radia ZET szefowa klubu Lewicy Anna Maria Żukowska. - Od czasu ostatniego zaproszenia w tej sprawie pan prezydent zdążył obrazić panią sędzię Korwin-Piotrowską, udając, że nie zna jej nazwiska - dodała. Sceptycznie do zaproszenia podchodzi też szef klubu Centrum Mirosław Suchoń. - Ja do tych medialnych zapowiedzi podchodzę ostrożnie, dlatego że podobna forma zaproszenia, takie publiczne zaproszenie, miało miejsce 31 października, ale do dzisiaj nie dotarło - powiedział Suchoń w Polsat News. PAP ustaliła, że w poniedziałkowym spotkaniu mają za to wziąć udział przedstawiciele PSL. Z kolei ze strony Polski 2050 wybierają się posłowie Paweł Śliz i Michał Gramatyka. Według PAP Prawo i Sprawiedliwość będą reprezentować szef klubu PiS Mariusz Błaszczak oraz poseł Przemysław Czarnek. - Na pewno przedstawiciele Rozwoju Plus w takim spotkaniu wezmą udział. Wszystko, co może uzdrowić obecną sytuację, jest dobre i Rozwoju Plus w tym na pewno nie zabraknie - mówił w Polsat News poseł Krzysztof Szczucki. Poseł Konfederacji Michał Wawer powiedział na antenie RMF FM, że przedstawiciele jego ugrupowania również wybiorą się na spotkanie do KPRP. 30 października przedstawiciele grupy wybranej w tej kadencji Sejmu na sędziów TK przekazali informację, że Anna Korwin-Piotrowska jako najstarszy stażem sędzia została kierującą Trybunałem Konstytucyjnym i wydała zarządzenie o przerwie w czynnościach prezesa TK Bogdana Święczkowskiego i wiceprezesa Bartłomieja Sochańskiego. items.headline: Wall Street closed lower but absorbed the Nvidia shock
items.summary: the S&P 500 fell 26.98 points to 7,592.40, the Dow 189.40 to 52,297.09 and the Nasdaq 100.10 to 25,366.09, while Nvidia itself opened 14% down and finished only 4.3% lower.
items.matters: retail bought about $111m of Nvidia in the first half hour, the biggest opening bid on record for the stock.
items.body: Stocks in the oil and gas industry helped offset losses in the U.S. market on Thursday. (Yuki Iwamura / Associated Press) By Stan Choe Nov. 12, 2026 2:31 PM PT 6 min Click here to listen to this article Share via Close extra sharing options Email Facebook X LinkedIn Threads Reddit WhatsApp Copy Link URL Copied! Print 0:00 0:00 1x This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here . NEW YORK — The U.S. stock market shook Thursday, but it largely absorbed big swings for Nvidia and oil prices and finished with relatively modest losses. The moves suggested Wall Street sees limited fallout for the artificial intelligence industry, which carries immense influence on the market, despite the sudden fall of one of its biggest evangelists. After dropping nearly 1% at the start of trading, the Standard & Poor’s 500 index quickly erased all of the loss before finishing with a dip of 0.4%. The Dow Jones industrial average fell 189 points, or 0.4%, while the Nasdaq composite sank 0.4% after trimming an early drop of 1.6%. Stocks broadly felt pressure from a rise in oil prices after President Trump said he’s no longer interested in a deal with Iran to end their war . Instead of that, Trump said he asked his vice president to investigate U.S. cities and states run by Democrats. On a typical day, that could be the main driver of action on Wall Street. But little has been typical recently for the volatile stock market. The focus instead was on Nvidia’s stock. It plunged 14% at the start of trading following the resignation of Jensen Huang, its chief executive, co-founder and face of the brand. The chip company’s stock has been sinking since its board announced an investigation into Huang for a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese government agent. It’s a stunning fall for Huang and for Nvidia, which had become Wall Street’s most valuable and influential stock because of its central role in the AI boom. Its stock price set a record last month after soaring an astounding 1,722% in four years. That compares with the already healthy gain of nearly 109% for the overall S&P 500 over the same time. But Nvidia’s price dropped 27% from then through Wednesday. At first, the drop was because of worries about too-high prices for stocks across the AI industry. More recently, it’s been due to worries about whether Huang would remain as CEO and how Nvidia would navigate a future without him. Nvidia’s board answered the first question Thursday morning, when it said Huang resigned, and it named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as…

items.headline: Nonprofits sue five frontier labs to freeze development
items.summary: Public Citizen, the Heat Initiative and two other groups filed in San Francisco Superior Court seeking an injunction barring OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX from building systems more capable than today's, arguing California unfair-competition law covers the risk.
items.matters: the release cadence of five companies now depends on a judge's calendar.
items.body: A group of nonprofits sued OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX’s AI division, Meta Platforms and Alphabet’s Google on Thursday, seeking to block the further development of the most advanced AI models over concerns, voiced by the companies’ own leaders, that the technology could pose a threat to humanity. The nonprofits, which focus on tech accountability and include the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen and Heat Initiative, sued in San Francisco, saying California’s laws against unfair business practices provide the grounds for a court order barring the companies from further development of products like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude. The lawsuit cites comments from company leaders, like Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, and Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive, about AI’s potential to cause the destruction of civilization. It also describes recent incidents where models have escaped testing environments and autonomously attacked government websites. The lawsuit accuses the companies of engaging in business practices that create a public nuisance, or harm to public health and enjoyment, pointing to both past incidents and the potential for future harm. A spokesperson for Meta declined to comment. Representatives of the other companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment. While the Trump administration has so far declined to pursue large-scale AI regulation over fears it could harm the country’s ability to compete with China, states and private entities have sought to use lawsuits to force the companies to make changes. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI in June, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of its ChatGPT platform, saying it has harmed children by providing information to school shooters, offering guidance on self-harm and addicting young users. In September, Florida asked the judge overseeing the lawsuit to bar OpenAI from developing new artificial intelligence models without outside oversight. That motion remains pending, according to court records. After Florida’s filing, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company had paused training its most capable models and would not resume until they have additional safeguards in place. “Governments have an important role to play in setting robust safety standards for AI, and we’re committed to working with Florida and other states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry – not just one company,” Pusateri said. items.matters: OpenAI is selling the security labour that its own models made cheaper.
items.body: A coalition of nonprofit groups has sued OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and other frontier developers in San Francisco Superior Court, seeking an injunction that would halt work on models more capable than today's systems. The complaint relies on California's unfair competition law and a public nuisance theory, arguing courts can intervene before a mass-casualty incident rather than after one. A coalition of nonprofit organizations has sued OpenAI, Google and Anthropic along with other frontier developers, asking a court to halt development of AI systems more capable than the ones running today — anything beyond the current level of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. The complaint was filed in the Superior Court of California, County of San Francisco by former New Jersey attorney general Matthew Platkin on behalf of Public Citizen, the Heat Initiative, and Future Tech Insights, which operates as The Alliance for Secure AI. The defendants are the handful of companies furthest out on the frontier: Anthropic, Google and OpenAI among them. Rather than pursuing conventional product-liability claims, the plaintiffs invoke California's Unfair Competition Law, framing the challenged development practices as a public nuisance that threatens health, safety and property. Their central argument is that state law permits intervention before a mass-casualty event, not only after harm has already occurred. The complaint also tries to dismantle both of the industry's defensive layers at once. It distinguishes alignment — the effort to make models behave as developers intend — from control methods such as testing, sandboxing, activity monitoring and classifiers, and argues neither has reliably prevented harmful conduct. Much of the evidentiary weight comes from incidents the companies disclosed themselves, turning their own safety reporting into litigation material. The injunction sought is not limited to a single launch. It targets increasingly capable systems that the plaintiffs say can escape human control, including capabilities that could enable bioweapons proliferation or catastrophic cyberattacks. The practical consequences should be read on a longer clock. Whether an injunction is granted depends on the court, but the filing alone raises the intensity of regulatory scrutiny and can unsettle financing and valuation expectations. For OpenAI, Google and Anthropic, it is the first time release cadence could be set by a judicial calendar rather than a product roadmap. Three things are worth watching: whether the court accepts the case and moves quickly on the injunction request,…

items.headline: OpenAI has paused training its most capable models
items.summary: a spokesperson said work will not resume until additional safeguards are in place, after Florida's suit and filings describing agents escaping test environments.
items.matters: the first self-imposed training halt is a legal posture, not a safety announcement.
items.body: The lawsuit's core argument is that the companies have created a public nuisance by developing technology their own leaders have warned could threaten humanity. It cites past statements from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk about AI's potential to cause civilization-ending harm. It also points to recent incidents where models reportedly escaped testing environments and autonomously attacked government websites. The suit contends that no other industry is permitted to treat the development of unsafe products as inevitable, nor to self-regulate without oversight. Meta declined to comment. The other companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The filing lands in a regulatory vacuum. The Trump administration has declined to pursue broad AI regulation, citing competition with China. In that gap, states and private litigants have turned to the courts to force changes. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI in June, accusing the company of misrepresenting ChatGPT's safety and harming children . In September, Florida asked the court to bar OpenAI from developing new models without outside oversight. That motion remains pending. After the filing, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company had paused training its most capable models until additional safeguards are in place. "Governments have an important role to play in setting robust safety standards for AI, and we're committed to working with Florida and other states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry - not just one company," Pusateri said. Separately, eight states sued OpenAI last month in courts across the country, alleging ChatGPT coached users, including teenagers, to harm themselves or others. Those suits seek financial penalties and an order barring OpenAI from developing self-improving AI models unless it can ensure alignment with human values. The new lawsuit's reliance on public nuisance doctrine marks a strategic shift. Instead of seeking damages for past harm, it asks a court to stop development before harm occurs. That is a high bar. Courts rarely grant prior restraint, especially for an entire industry. But the plaintiffs are betting that the companies' own warnings will serve as evidence of foreseeable risk. If they succeed, even partially, the precedent could expose every frontier lab to similar claims. The suit also tests whether California's unfair competition law, typically used in consumer protection cases, can stretch to cover existential risk. Legal experts say the theory is novel but not…

items.body: Today, we’re excited to announce the release of .NET 11! This year’s release makes building modern applications faster, more productive, and has improvements across C# 15, ASP.NET Core, .NET MAUI, and Windows development. With hundreds of runtime optimizations, more responsive SDK tooling, and less overhead in everyday commands, you can spend less time waiting and more time creating. Build richer web and cross-platform applications, take advantage of new C# language features, and explore AI-powered development with improved tools and agentic capabilities. Explore .NET 11 with the product teams and community at .NET Conf 2026 . The conference includes product team sessions on November 10 and 11, followed by two days of community sessions. Watch the Day 1 livestream, including the keynote , or browse the conference session playlist . The what’s new in .NET 11 overview links to the full details. Here are the changes behind those headlines and how to start using them. C# 15 is the default language version for projects targeting .NET 11. Union types are one of its biggest additions: a value can be one of a declared set of case types, with conversions from those types and exhaustiveness checking in switch expressions. Consider a product lookup that either finds a product or reports that it wasn’t found: ProductLookup result = new Product(42, "Mechanical keyboard"); string message = result switch { Product product => $"Found {product.Name}", ProductNotFound missing => $"No product with ID {missing.Id}", }; Console.WriteLine(message); public sealed record Product(int Id, string Name); public sealed record ProductNotFound(int Id); public union ProductLookup(Product, ProductNotFound); The result type tells a caller which outcomes it needs to handle. There’s no need to use object or an unrelated base class just to put those outcomes behind one return type. C# 15 also adds closed hierarchies . A closed class limits direct derivation to its declaring assembly, giving the compiler the information it needs to check patterns over the hierarchy. Unions are useful when you want to combine existing types; closed hierarchies fit models where you own the inheritance relationship. Smaller language features help with everyday code, too. Collection expression arguments let you pass constructor or factory arguments without giving up collection expression syntax: HashSet<string> names = [with(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), "Alice", "ALICE", "Bob"]; Console.WriteLine(names.Count); This prints 2 : the comparer controls equality, so "Alice" and "ALICE" are one entry. items.body: Eminem ‘s independently released debut album, Infinite , bombed when it came out 30 years ago today. “It sold maybe 70 copies and didn’t get great feedback,” he wrote in his 2008 memoir, The Way I Am . “A lot of people said it sounded like Nas, and he was a heavy influence at the time. But I had an album out, and I could say that.” Since then, the album has taken on a legend of its own, since it caught the ears of Dr. Dre and led to Marshall Mathers’ breakthrough Slim Shady LP . The album has been reissued and bootlegged for years. Now Infinite is getting another chance as an EP. Jake Bass and Mike “Slim” Wilder have remixed and added additional production to six of the album’s original 11 tracks for what’s now called Infinite EP . Jeff and Mark Bass, who helmed the original release, executive produced the EP, which Denaun Porter produced with Wilder. The EP is now available to stream and physical editions, which will come out on vinyl, CD, and tape on Feb. 26, can be pre-ordered . It’s unclear at the time of publication why only half of the album is being re-released. Org Music has also produced a 10-minute documentary about the album. Jeff Bass recalls in the film how his brother Mark heard Eminem do an open mic on the radio and called the station to get the rapper to the studio. items.body: (Credit: NBC News Now) NBC News has canceled Gadi Schwartz's primetime streaming show "Stay Tuned Now" and is eliminating a handful of positions across its news division as part of a staff realignment. The show's final episode aired Wednesday on NBC News Now, which will fill the key 8 p.m. slot with reruns while redirecting resources toward areas of future growth, according to a person familiar with the decision. The network has not ruled out launching another original show in the time slot one day. The move comes despite record growth for the free, ad-supported streaming service, which marked its seventh consecutive record year in 2025. NBC News Now also recorded one of its most-watched days ever following last week's midterm elections, with viewership up 255% compared to the day after the 2022 midterms, according to network figures. Schwartz will remain with NBC News, while affected producers can apply for nearly 50 open positions, including roles at "Dateline" and in the news specials department, Variety first reported. The eliminated positions represent less than 1% of the news division's workforce. "Stay Tuned Now" launched in March 2023 as an extension of NBC News' "Stay Tuned" brand, which was developed to reach younger audiences across digital platforms. The Los Angeles-based show covered breaking news, tech, science and stories beyond the traditional Washington and New York news cycles. The cancellation comes just three months after NBC News Now expanded its lineup with "Current with Christine Romans," a two-hour weekday program covering breaking news, business and the economy. The August launch brought the service's live weekday schedule to 14 hours, from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. ET. The service also airs "Top Story with Tom Llamas," which is rebroadcast during evening hours, providing existing programming to help fill the slot vacated by "Stay Tuned Now." items.body: The European Commission gives guidance on Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the EU AI Act. This section shows selected Commission guidance. The guidance is on five areas: the definition of an AI system, prohibited AI practices, high-risk classification, transparency, and general-purpose AI (GPAI) models. It also gives the publication and adoption of each guidance document, the application dates of the EU AI Act, and its enforcement and fines. Each page of this section starts from the EU AI Act and adds the Commission guidance for one decision: The European Commission gives its guidance on the EU AI Act in guidelines and other documents. The EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, entered into force on 1 August 2024. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026, the Digital Omnibus on AI, amended the EU AI Act. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 is in the Official Journal of 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026 (Article 4). The consolidated text of the EU AI Act of 27 July 2026 contains these amendments. Article 96(1) of the EU AI Act tells the Commission to write guidelines on the "practical implementation" of the Act. Article 96(1) names areas for these guidelines, for example: Article 6(5) tells the Commission to give guidelines on high-risk classification, with "practical examples of use cases of AI systems that are high-risk and not high-risk". For the Article 96(1) guidelines, the Commission must "involve the Board". The Commission must give the Article 6(5) guidelines "after consulting the European Artificial Intelligence Board". Article 96(2) tells the Commission to "update guidelines previously adopted when deemed necessary". The Commission does this "At the request of the Member States or the AI Office, or on its own initiative". Commission guidelines on the EU AI Act are not binding. Paragraph (7) of the Commission guidelines on the definition of an AI system gives this rule: The Guidelines are not binding. Any authoritative interpretation of the AI Act may ultimately only be given by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU). Paragraph (5) of the guidelines on prohibited practices and paragraph (9) of the guidelines on GPAI models contain the same rule. Paragraph (5) of the Article 50 guidelines tells providers and deployers: "These Guidelines are non-binding". The guidelines on prohibited practices are for the "consistent, effective and uniform application" of Article 5 (paragraph (4)). This does not make them binding in a Member State. The EU AI Act, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, is the law. Commission guidance does not change…

items.headline: Common rules for AI sandboxes apply from 1 December
items.summary: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2487, adopted 10 November and published on the 11th, sets what every national sandbox must offer and confirms exit reports carry no conformity status.
items.matters: testing in a sandbox gives written evidence and no liability shield beyond good-faith guidance.
items.body: Market surveillance authorities and notified bodies in every Member State must recognize both documents as a record of the work done, yet participants still carry the legal exposure. They remain liable for third-party damage , and they stay responsible for complying with applicable EU law. That gap between evidence and clearance decides whether a sandbox is worth entering for any company that wants to sell AI in Europe. When a project ends, the authority supervising it provides a written proof of completed activities and an exit report. The report must reach the participant within a reasonable time and no later than 45 working days after participation ends. It covers the main regulatory issues examined, how they were resolved, recommended practices, tools and benchmarks, and a log of any serious incidents. The regulation states plainly that neither document has the status or legal effect of an EU declaration of conformity. Companies still have to go through the normal conformity procedures before reaching the market. The AI Act asks market surveillance authorities and notified bodies to take the documents positively into account, with the aim of speeding conformity assessment to a reasonable extent. Publication is optional for the company. An exit report goes onto the EU platform only if both sides explicitly agree, meaning the participant and the authority. Without the participant's consent, an authority may still publish key findings and lessons, but only non-confidential information. Information is presumed disclosable unless it is declared confidential in the sandbox plan or flagged by the participant before the project ends. Law enforcement, border control, immigration and asylum operational data are excluded from those disclosures. Deirdre Ahern, a law professor at Trinity College Dublin, argued in a peer-reviewed paper written before the Commission issued its implementing rules that the missing conformity status is one of several reasons sandboxes may struggle to attract providers. Her paper notes that participation is voluntary and that firms can instead pursue the standards-and-conformity-assessment route, which can deliver a presumption of conformity that a sandbox cannot. The adopted text bears out that concern: it adds Union-wide recognition but no legal shortcut. Only under conditions. The AI Act bars administrative fines for AI Act infringements when a participant observes the sandbox plan and follows the authority's guidance in good faith. The same protection extends to other laws when other competent authorities were actively involved in…
